extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent application's specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA §112), including examiner procedures for rejections, handling replies, and assessing genus/species support and priority claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession of the claimed invention — factors to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification shows that applicant was in possession of the claimed invention is ... a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to be considered include the level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention. Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to the conclusion that the applicant was in possession of the claimed species is sufficient. (See Eli Lilly, In re Hayes, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirement varies with art maturity and invention scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The description needed to satisfy the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112 “varies with the nature and scope of the invention at issue, and with the scientific and technologic knowledge already in existence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents and printed publications in the art should be relied upon to determine whether an art is mature and what the level of knowledge and skill is in the art. The amount and type of disclosure required depends on that context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/method disclosure may suffice in mature arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In most technologies which are mature ... a written description question should not be raised for claims present in the application when originally filed, even if the specification discloses only a method of making the invention and the function of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Disclosing a microprocessor capable of performing certain functions is sufficient when one skilled in the art would understand what is intended and know how to carry it out (In re Hayes). An inventor is not required to describe every detail in a mature art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher specificity required in emerging or unpredictable arts
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions in emerging and unpredictable technologies, or for inventions characterized by factors not reasonably predictable ... more evidence is required to show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of only a method of making the invention and the function may not be sufficient to support a product claim other than a product-by-process claim. Where the process has actually been used to produce the product, product-by-process written description may be satisfied; otherwise additional proof of operability or ability to carry out the process is required. (See Fiers v. Revel; Amgen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial-structure disclosure insufficient without additional characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization of the product may not be sufficient to evidence possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In chemical and biological arts (e.g., genes), conception requires the inventor be able to define the compound so as to distinguish it, or describe how to obtain it, or provide physical/chemical properties or other characteristics; defining solely by principal biological property (e.g., encoding erythropoietin) is insufficient. Reduction to practice may be the only corroborating evidence. (See Amgen; Burroughs Wellcome.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Species claims must meet the applicable tests or be rejected
rubrics_metrics.description: Any claim to a species that does not meet the test described under at least one of (a), (b), or (c) must be rejected as lacking adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (The MPEP/earlier sections define the referenced tests (a)-(c).) Examiner should apply those tests and reject species claims that fail to meet them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claims: support via representative species or identifying characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement for a claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species ... or by disclosure of relevant, identifying characteristics, i.e., structure or other physical and/or chemical properties, by functional characteristics coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between function and structure, or by a combination of such identifying characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A “representative number of species” means the species which are adequately described are representative of the entire genus. When there is substantial variation within the genus, one must describe a sufficient variety of species to reflect that variation. Disclosure of only one species may be adequate only if it “indicates that the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the gen[us].” Cases (Enzo Biochem, Noelle v. Lederman, In re Curtis, etc.) illustrate when one species suffices and when it does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes a representative number is inverse to skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes a “representative number” is an inverse function of the skill and knowledge in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfactory disclosure depends on whether one skilled in the art would recognize that the applicant was in possession of the necessary common attributes or features possessed by the members of the genus in view of the species disclosed. In unpredictable arts, disclosing only one species generally will not achieve adequate written description for a broad genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification cannot support expansive claim language merely by describing one embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification cannot always support expansive claim language and satisfy the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112 “merely by clearly describing one embodiment of the thing claimed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issue is whether a person skilled in the art would understand applicant to have invented, and been in possession of, the invention as broadly claimed. If the specification teaches only one particular method and there is no evidence it contemplates a more generic method, broader claims may be invalid (LizardTech v. Earth Resource Mapping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner initial burden and required findings for rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting evidence or reasoning to explain why persons skilled in the art would not recognize in the original disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rejecting a claim, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact which should: (A) Identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) Establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time of filing would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the disclosure. A general allegation of “unpredictability in the art” is not sufficient. (See Wertheim.) When appropriate, suggest amendments to the claims which can be supported by the application’s written description, being mindful of the prohibition against addition of new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for new or amended claims and priority claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with the written description requirement ... or to be entitled to an earlier priority date or filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, or 365(c), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an explicit limitation is not present in the written description whose benefit is sought, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood at the time of filing that the description requires that limitation. Inherency must be established by clear extrinsic evidence (not probabilities). If support is lacking, an amended/new claim must be rejected or priority denied. (See Hyatt v. Boone; In re Robertson; In re Wright; In re Robins.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must include elements described as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Furthermore, each claim must include all elements which applicant has described as essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an element which applicant describes as essential or critical is not claimed, a new or amended claim must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as lacking adequate written description. (See Johnson Worldwide Assoc. Inc. v. Zebco Corp.; Gentry Gallery v. Berkline Corp.; Tronzo v. Biomet.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete patentability determination and clear communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all the relevant statutory provisions of title 35 of the U.S. Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After analyzing the claimed invention under 101, 112, 102, and 103, review all proposed rejections and their bases to confirm correctness before imposing any rejection. The Office action should clearly communicate the findings, conclusions, and reasons which support them, and when possible offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination practice on reply by applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon reply by applicant, before repeating any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) ... review the basis for the rejection in view of the record as a whole, including amendments, arguments, and any evidence submitted by applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the whole record now demonstrates that the written description requirement is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If not, repeat the rejection, fully respond to applicant’s rebuttal arguments, and properly treat any further showings submitted in the reply. When a rejection is maintained, any affidavits relevant to the written description requirement must be thoroughly analyzed and discussed in the next Office action. (See In re Alton.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish written description issues from new matter objections
rubrics_metrics.description: A written description requirement issue generally involves whether the subject matter of a claim is supported by the disclosure of an application as filed. The claim should not be rejected or objected to on the ground of new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concept of new matter is properly employed as a basis for objection to amendments to the abstract, specification or drawings attempting to add new disclosure to that originally presented. While the test or analysis of description requirement and new matter issues is the same, the examining procedure and statutory basis for addressing these issues differ. See MPEP § 2163.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective standard for written description sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: An objective standard: “does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Vas-Cath, to satisfy the written description requirement, an applicant must convey with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, he or she was in possession of the invention, and that the invention is whatever is now claimed. Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice, showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (drawings or structural chemical formulas), or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. Subject matter need not be literally described in haec verba; implicit or inherent support may suffice if a skilled artisan would understand it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical circumstances where written description issues arise
rubrics_metrics.description: A description requirement issue can arise in a number of circumstances where it must be determined whether the subject matter of a claim is supported in an application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most typically the issue arises when: I) an amendment affects a claim (claim amendments or specification amendments), II) reliance on filing date of a parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120, or III) reliance on priority under 35 U.S.C. 119. Rejection of an original claim for lack of written description should be rare due to a strong presumption that the specification as filed is adequate. (See In re Wertheim.)
